speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources in light of smoky chemical smells reported in parts of Singapore at end-September 2017 (a) what is the cause of the smell; (b) what are the standards and safety measures that operators of hazardous chemical installations, including the transportation of such materials, have to comply with to ensure that there are no lapses or leakages that may compromise public safety and health; and (c) whether other countries in Southeast Asia have similar standards and safety measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The National Environment Agency (NEA) maintains a network of real-time air quality monitoring stations across Singapore to detect air pollution.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A number of these stations can measure low levels of Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) in the air.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: VOCs are vapours which can come from both man-made and natural sources, and they can cause smells by themselves or when they react with other VOCs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA supplements the air monitoring stations by deploying officers to affected areas.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These officers are equipped with portable instruments which can measure the levels of chemical compounds in the air.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) is also equipped with portable sensors to detect and identify toxic gases, including chemical warfare agents, in the air.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the late afternoon of 25 September 2017, members of the public reported smells in the Punggol and Sengkang areas.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Similar reports were received from the northern and central parts of Singapore later in the evening, such as Ang Mo Kio, Toa Payoh and Bukit Timah.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Upon receipt of the public reports, officers from NEA and SCDF were immediately deployed to check that the air at the affected locations was safe.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The officers also conducted investigations at nearby housing estates, factories and construction sites.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The smell could also have been intensified by the light wind conditions during the period and only dissipated later that night when winds blowing from the south and southeast picked up strength.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While there have been previous smell-related incidents, this episode was more widely spread across the island.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In their investigations, NEA and SCDF did not detect any build-up of harmful gases in the air or find any abnormal factory operations or incidents that could have caused the smells.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Despite the increase, the levels of the VOCs detected were also well within international safety guidelines.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Once this was established, the public was informed that the air was safe.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the same time, NEA informed its counterparts from the Malaysian Department of Environment (DOE) in Johor of the incident and sought their assistance to locate the possible source of the smell.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Following NEA's request for assistance, the DOE in Johor deployed its assets to investigate the incident.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Malaysia media reported on 6 October 2017 that the stop work order was lifted after the operator had completed the necessary remedial actions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Tracing the source of fugitive smell is not a straight-forward process and requires time and effort.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: After NEA reached out to DOE, the Malaysians reacted quickly to carry out site investigation, trace the source of the smell and take the necessary actions on the facility to rectify the problem.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Industrial premises in Singapore must comply with strict regulations and guidelines on the storage and transportation of hazardous materials.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, the Environmental Protection and Management Act (EPMA) imposes requirements on the storage, use and transport of hazardous substances.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These include putting emergency plans in place and preparing adequate emergency response equipment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These control measures are similar to those adopted in other jurisdictions, with each country adapting them to local requirements.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our agencies are prepared for such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The SCDF regularly conducts exercises simulating chemical agent attacks where responders are tested for their proficiency in detection, monitoring and mitigation operations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In incidents involving toxic gases, the response of the public is equally important.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Those in the affected area may feel unwell or experience symptoms, such as giddiness and shortness of breath.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SCDF’s advice is that they should quickly leave the affected area and, where possible, help evacuate others, before seeking medical attention.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For those who are unable to leave the affected area, they should go to the nearest indoor area and adopt In-Place Protection Procedures (IPP) by shutting the doors, windows and ventilation systems, like fans and air conditioners, and sealing the gaps with masking tape to minimise the infiltration of hazardous vapours.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SCDF will also send out alerts to notify the public to take the necessary precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This alert will be sent out through all the public warning platforms, including social media, the SGSecure app and all the free-to-air frequency modulation (FM) radio and television channels.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The "Important Message" signal of the Public Warning System may also be activated.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To learn more about how to respond in the event of an incident involving toxic gases, the public is encouraged to participate in the SCDF’s Community Emergency Preparedness Programme (CEPP).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: CEPP trains about 40,000 participants each year, and IPP is one of the advanced programme modules.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Members of the public can learn to prepare an IPP kit, as well as how they can apply IPP against a chemical gas attack.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More information on IPP can be found in the Civil Defence Emergency Handbook, which can be downloaded from the SCDF website.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are among the measures that NEA and SCDF have put in place to safeguard the health and safety of Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just now, the Minister mentioned that the test showed that the air was safe.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the northern part of Singapore like Yishun, we will be affected first if there is anything that comes from Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Certainly, we have enough of these and if we find that we need to build more of such monitoring stations on the advice of consultants or otherwise, we will do so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I understand that it takes time to trace the source of the noxious smell in the air, but I think our residents will appreciate a timely update on what chemicals are in the air, to aid their own assessment of what they can do to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And my question is whether there is any research done on long-term exposure to low levels of VOCs in the air.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I asked this because residents in Punggol and Sengkang obviously live closer to Pasir Gudang, and there are a lot of feedback or persistent concerns about such chemicals in the air.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though at any one point in time, such VOC levels may be low and not cause immediate alarm, long-term exposure to VOCs may cause and endanger health.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Studies which are connected with low constant exposure to these VOCs are not yet available or have not been done, so we cannot rely on such reports to produce any guidelines for our authorities to implement.
